title: Histology of the Heart and Blood Vessels
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the microscopic structure of the heart wall, the cardiac muscle cell, the conducting and endocrine cells of the heart, the walls of each class of blood vessel, and the products of the endothelium. Part I questions rarely stop at identification; they ask what a layer or cell does, what happens when it fails, and which disease begins there. The organizing idea is that structure follows demand: the left ventricle is thick to generate systemic pressure, the fibrous skeleton is collagen to anchor valves and block current, the aorta is elastic to smooth pulsatile flow, arterioles are muscular to set resistance, and capillaries are thin to exchange.
prerequisites: The four basic tissue types and the general organization of epithelium and connective tissue
Sarcomere structure and the sliding filament mechanism in striated muscle
Cell junctions: adherens junctions, desmosomes, tight junctions, and gap junctions
Gross anatomy of the heart chambers, valves, and great vessels (CV-3)
Second messenger signaling through cAMP, cGMP, and IP3 with Ca2+

connections.how: The insulating fibrous skeleton and fast Purkinje fibers explain AV nodal delay, a narrow QRS, and preexcitation through accessory pathways.
Elastic recoil of large arteries, arteriolar resistance, and venous compliance become the pressure, flow, and capacitance relationships of the circulation.
The subendocardium is the layer most vulnerable to ischemia, and endothelial dysfunction starts the plaque that narrows epicardial coronary arteries.
Atherosclerosis begins in the intima, cystic medial degeneration and dissection involve the media, and syphilitic aortitis begins in the vasa vasorum.
Endothelial von Willebrand factor, thrombomodulin, and prostacyclin start the platelet and coagulation pathways, and ADAMTS13 deficiency causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

terms.def: The inner layer of the heart wall: endothelium on a thin connective tissue layer, with a subendocardial layer that carries vessels, nerves, and Purkinje fibers.
Dense irregular connective tissue forming the fibrous rings around the four valve orifices, the fibrous trigones, and the membranous septum.
The right fibrous trigone, the thickest part of the cardiac skeleton, which the bundle of His pierces to reach the ventricles.
The specialized end to end junction between cardiac muscle cells, containing fascia adherens, desmosomes, and gap junctions.
A cluster of connexon channels (connexin 43 in working ventricular muscle) that lets ions and small molecules pass directly between neighboring cells.
A tissue of separate cells that behaves electrically like a single cell because gap junctions spread depolarization from cell to cell.
The pairing of one T tubule with one terminal cistern of sarcoplasmic reticulum, located at the Z line in ventricular cardiac muscle.
A large, pale, glycogen rich conducting cell with few myofibrils that lies in the subendocardium and rapidly distributes the impulse through the ventricles.
A peptide hormone stored in granules of atrial muscle cells and released by atrial stretch, which promotes Na+ and water excretion and relaxes vascular smooth muscle.
A fenestrated sheet of elastin that forms the outer boundary of the tunica intima in arteries and is most distinct in muscular arteries.
Small vessels in the adventitia and outer media of large vessels that supply the part of the wall too far from the lumen to be fed by diffusion.
A rod shaped endothelial storage granule containing von Willebrand factor and P-selectin that is released within minutes of endothelial activation.

sections.title: Layers of the heart wall and the fibrous cardiac skeleton

blocks.text: The heart wall layers match those of a vessel: endocardium (intima), myocardium (media), and epicardium (adventitia). The fibrous cardiac skeleton has no vascular counterpart.
Endocardium and valves

The endocardium is a simple squamous endothelium, continuous with that of the great vessels, on thin connective tissue. Its deepest part, the subendocardial layer, carries small vessels, nerves, and the Purkinje fibers. Valve leaflets are folds of endocardium around an essentially avascular core: a collagenous fibrosa, continuous with the fibrous ring, bears the load, a proteoglycan rich spongiosa cushions flexion, and an elastic layer lies on the inflow side. Proteoglycan expansion of the spongiosa is the lesion of myxomatous mitral valve (prolapse), and vessels growing into scarred leaflets mark chronic rheumatic disease.
Myocardium

Myocardial thickness follows chamber pressure: atria a few millimeters, right ventricle about 0.3 to 0.5 cm, left ventricle about 1.3 to 1.5 cm. By the law of Laplace, wall stress is proportional to pressure times radius divided by twice the wall thickness, so a thicker wall keeps the stress on each myocyte tolerable. Pressure overload (hypertension, aortic stenosis) adds sarcomeres in parallel and causes concentric hypertrophy; volume overload (regurgitation) adds them in series and causes eccentric hypertrophy with a larger cavity. Hypertrophied myocytes have large, dark, rectangular boxcar nuclei.

blocks.title: Wall stress and the purpose of hypertrophy
blocks.text: A left ventricle with a radius of 2.5 cm and a wall of 1.0 cm at 120 mmHg has stress proportional to (120 x 2.5) / (2 x 1.0) = 150 units. If aortic stenosis raises systolic pressure to 200 mmHg, stress rises to 250 units. Thickening the wall to about 1.7 cm restores it to about 147 units, but the thicker wall is stiffer and outgrows its capillary supply, predisposing to subendocardial ischemia. A dilated ventricle with a radius of 3.5 cm and a wall of 0.8 cm at 120 mmHg has a stress of about 263 units, so dilation without matching hypertrophy sharply raises the energy cost of each beat.
The inner third of the left ventricular wall, the subendocardium, is the layer most vulnerable to ischemia, so a subendocardial infarct can occur without total occlusion of an artery.

blocks.title: Why the subendocardium is injured first
steps: Coronary arteries run in epicardial fat and penetrate inward
Systole raises intramural pressure most near the cavity
Inner wall vessels are compressed, so inner flow is mainly diastolic
Wall stress and O2 demand are highest in the inner layers
Hypotension, tachycardia, or hypertrophy drops supply below demand
Necrosis appears first in the inner third of the wall
blocks.caption: The subendocardium is the watershed of the ventricular wall.

blocks.text: Epicardium

The epicardium is the visceral serous pericardium: mesothelium over fat that carries the coronary vessels and nerves, hence epicardial coronary disease. Roughened mesothelium in pericarditis produces a friction rub.
Fibrous cardiac skeleton

The skeleton is dense irregular connective tissue, mainly type I collagen: four fibrous rings around the valve orifices, the right and left fibrous trigones, and the membranous interventricular septum. The right trigone, the thickest part, is the central fibrous body. It anchors the valves and myocardial sheets and completely separates atrial from ventricular muscle. Collagen has no gap junctions, so atrial depolarization stops at the rings. The only normal crossing is the bundle of His, which leaves the AV node, pierces the central fibrous body, and runs along the membranous septum, so every impulse passes the slow AV node and its delay (CV-7).

A strand of myocardium crossing a ring forms an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) that bypasses AV delay, giving a short PR interval, a delta wave, and reentrant tachycardia (Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern). Because the His bundle lies beside the aortic ring and membranous septum, an aortic valve ring abscess in infective endocarditis, ring calcification, or surgery there can cause new AV block.

sections.title: Cardiac muscle cells compared with skeletal muscle

blocks.text: Cardiomyocytes contain the same sarcomeres as skeletal muscle and are striated, but they differ in shape, junctions, and Ca2+ handling because the heart must contract as one unit, beat for a lifetime, and grade its force without recruiting more cells.

A ventricular myocyte is a short branched cylinder, about 10 to 20 micrometers wide and 80 to 100 micrometers long, with one or two central nuclei. A clear perinuclear zone holds the Golgi apparatus, glycogen, and lipofuscin, a wear and tear pigment that accumulates with age. Mitochondria fill about a third or more of the cell, with close to one capillary per myocyte, because the heart makes nearly all its ATP by oxidative phosphorylation, mainly of fatty acids. Contraction stops within about a minute of complete ischemia, and irreversible injury begins after roughly 20 to 40 minutes.
Intercalated discs

Myocytes join end to end at intercalated discs, dark stepped lines across the fiber. The transverse portion, at the level of a Z line, holds the mechanical junctions; the lateral portion holds most of the gap junctions.

blocks.title: Junctions of the intercalated disc
rows: Cadherins linked to actin of the last sarcomere
Transmits contractile pull to the next cell; replaces the Z line at the cell end
Desmosomal cadherins linked to desmin through plakoglobin, plakophilin, and desmoplakin
Keeps cells from pulling apart under repeated stress
Connexons of connexin 43 in ventricular muscle
Passes ions between cells, making the myocardium a functional syncytium
blocks.caption: Two junctions couple cells mechanically and one couples them electrically.

blocks.text: Gap junctions let depolarizing current flow from cell to cell, so excitation crosses a chamber in a fraction of a second and travels faster along the fiber axis than across it. At the border of an old infarct or in a failing ventricle, gap junctions are reduced or shifted to the lateral cell borders, which slows conduction and creates a substrate for reentry. Mutations in desmosomal proteins such as plakophilin 2 or desmoplakin cause arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy: myocytes detach under stretch and are replaced by fibrofatty tissue, mostly in the right ventricle, causing ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death in young people. Naxos disease, a recessive plakoglobin defect, adds woolly hair and thickened palm and sole skin because the same desmosomal protein holds the epidermis together.
Ca2+ handling and repair

In cardiac muscle the L-type Ca2+ channel of the T tubule admits extracellular Ca2+ during the plateau, and that Ca2+ opens ryanodine receptor 2 in the adjacent cistern (calcium induced calcium release). Because force depends on Ca2+ entry and SR loading, it can be graded, and the long refractory period prevents tetanus (CV-5). Atrial myocytes have few T tubules. Adult cardiomyocytes are essentially postmitotic and have no satellite cell reserve, so the heart adapts by hypertrophy and heals infarcts with collagen scar.

blocks.predict: A child has greatly reduced ventricular connexin 43 but normal desmosomes and fascia adherens. Would the cells pull apart, and how would excitation spread?
blocks.explain: The cells stay attached because adhesion depends on the desmosomes and fascia adherens. Excitation spreads slowly and irregularly because current passes between myocytes mainly through gap junctions, a substrate for reentrant arrhythmias.

sections.title: Purkinje fibers and atrial natriuretic peptide granules

blocks.text: The conducting cells and the atrial endocrine cells are modified cardiomyocytes that trade contractile machinery for speed or hormone secretion, and their histology shows the trade.
Purkinje fibers

Purkinje fibers form a network in the subendocardium of both ventricles, continuous with the bundle branches. They are larger than working myocytes, with pale glycogen rich cytoplasm (PAS positive), a few myofibrils pushed to the periphery, and one or two central nuclei often ringed by a clear halo. Their large diameter lowers internal resistance to longitudinal current, abundant gap junctions lower resistance between cells, and a large fast Na+ current drives depolarization. Conduction is therefore the fastest in the heart, about 1.5 to 4 m/s, so the ventricles depolarize almost together and the normal QRS is narrow.

Glycogen supports anaerobic glycolysis, which is thought to help Purkinje fibers tolerate ischemia; together with diffusion from cavity blood this lets surviving fibers at the inner edge of an infarct become a source of ectopic beats. Purkinje fibers also pace at about 20 to 40 beats per minute, the wide complex ventricular escape rhythm (CV-7). The cerebellar Purkinje neuron is an unrelated cell and a common matching trap.

blocks.title: Purkinje fibers, working myocytes, and nodal cells
rows: Smallest; pale, in dense connective tissue
About 0.05 m/s in the AV node
blocks.caption: Purkinje fibers are built for speed and nodal cells for pacing and delay. Velocities are approximate.

blocks.text: Atrial granules and natriuretic peptides

Electron micrographs of atrial myocytes, most numerous in the right atrium, show membrane bound dense granules near the nucleus and Golgi apparatus. They store atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), released when increased volume or pressure stretches the atrium, which makes the heart an endocrine organ. Ventricular myocytes make B type natriuretic peptide (BNP) mainly on demand in response to wall stretch rather than storing it in prominent granules, which is why plasma BNP or NT-proBNP rises in heart failure.

ANP binds natriuretic peptide receptor A, which has its own guanylyl cyclase domain, so its second messenger is cGMP. It dilates the afferent and constricts the efferent arteriole to raise GFR, inhibits collecting duct Na+ reabsorption, suppresses renin and aldosterone, and relaxes vascular smooth muscle.

sections.title: Wall structure of arteries, capillaries, and veins

blocks.text: Arteries and veins have an intima (endothelium and thin subendothelial tissue, bounded in arteries by the internal elastic lamina), a media of smooth muscle and the matrix it secretes, and a mainly collagenous adventitia carrying nerves and, in large vessels, the vasa vasorum, which feed the outer wall beyond the reach of luminal diffusion and are more plentiful in veins.

One or two smooth muscle layers; elastic lamina only in larger ones
Endothelium and basal lamina with pericytes only
Thin media; intimal folds form valves
Thin media; adventitia thickest, with longitudinal muscle
blocks.caption: Arteries are built around the media; large veins are built around the adventitia.

blocks.text: Arteries and arterioles
In systole the aorta stretches and stores ejection energy; in diastole it recoils, maintaining diastolic pressure and nearly continuous distal flow (the windkessel effect).

blocks.title: Elastic recoil of the aorta
steps: Left ventricle ejects a stroke volume into the aorta
Elastic lamellae stretch and store ejection energy
Systolic pressure rises less than in a rigid tube
Aortic valve closes; the stretched wall recoils
Diastolic pressure and distal flow are maintained
blocks.caption: Loss of elastin raises systolic pressure, lowers diastolic pressure, and widens pulse pressure.

blocks.text: With age, elastin fragments and is replaced by collagen, causing isolated systolic hypertension. In Marfan syndrome, defective fibrillin 1 weakens elastin, producing cystic medial degeneration, aortic root dilation, and dissection, which splits the media. In tertiary syphilis, obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum makes the outer media ischemic, and the ascending aorta becomes aneurysmal with a tree bark intima. Atherosclerosis affects the intima of elastic and muscular arteries, whereas Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis calcifies the internal elastic lamina and media of muscular arteries, giving pipestem calcification without narrowing the lumen.

Arterioles (generally under about 0.1 mm) are the main resistance vessels because resistance varies with the inverse fourth power of radius: a 20% narrowing raises resistance about 2.4 times. Pressure falls more across them than anywhere else, from about 85 to about 30 to 35 mmHg. Hyaline arteriolosclerosis (hypertension, diabetes) deposits leaked plasma protein in the wall, and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis of severe hypertension adds concentric onion skin smooth muscle; both narrow the lumen and reduce renal perfusion.
Capillaries, venules, and veins
Capillaries are about 5 to 10 micrometers wide, and their huge total cross section slows flow for exchange.

blocks.title: The three types of capillary
rows: Unbroken endothelium and basal lamina; transport vesicles
Muscle, lung, connective tissue, nervous system
Water, gases, small solutes; tight junctions form the blood brain barrier
Pores about 60 to 80 nm, usually with a diaphragm; continuous basal lamina
Endocrine glands, intestinal villi, choroid plexus, kidney
Fluid, hormones, nutrients; glomerular pores lack diaphragms
Wide lumen, large gaps, discontinuous basal lamina
blocks.caption: Permeability rises from continuous to fenestrated to sinusoidal.

blocks.text: Postcapillary venules are where leukocytes emigrate and where histamine and bradykinin open endothelial gaps, so inflammatory edema begins there; high endothelial venules admit lymphocytes to lymph nodes. Veins are thin walled and compliant and hold about 60% to 70% of blood volume. Limb vein valves, with the skeletal muscle pump, keep flow toward the heart; valves are absent from the venae cavae, portal system, and dural sinuses. Incompetent valves raise leg venous pressure and cause varicose veins.
Endothelial products control tone, platelets, coagulation, and leukocyte traffic. In health they favor relaxation and fluidity.
Nitric oxide

Endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) makes NO and L-citrulline from L-arginine and O2, using NADPH and tetrahydrobiopterin. Besides relaxing smooth muscle, NO inhibits platelet adhesion and aggregation, leukocyte adhesion, and smooth muscle proliferation. Superoxide and hemoglobin destroy it within seconds, so its action is local. Increased flow raises shear stress and releases NO, so the upstream artery widens (flow mediated dilation).

steps: Shear stress, acetylcholine, or bradykinin act on endothelium
Ca2+ with calmodulin, and phosphorylation, activate eNOS
NO diffuses into the underlying smooth muscle
Soluble guanylyl cyclase raises cGMP; protein kinase G activates
Ca2+ falls and myosin light chain phosphatase activates
Smooth muscle relaxes and the vessel dilates
blocks.caption: The same NO and cGMP signal inhibits platelets.

blocks.title: The acetylcholine paradox
blocks.text: Acetylcholine relaxes an artery with intact endothelium but contracts one whose endothelium has been rubbed away. In the intact vessel it binds endothelial M3 receptors, raises endothelial Ca2+, activates eNOS, and NO relaxes the muscle, outweighing its direct effect. Without endothelium it reaches only smooth muscle M3 receptors, which act through Gq, IP3, and Ca2+ to cause contraction. Infused into a human coronary artery, acetylcholine dilates a healthy vessel but constricts one with atherosclerosis or risk factor driven dysfunction, revealing lost bioavailable NO.
Prostacyclin, endothelin-1, and Weibel-Palade bodies

Endothelial prostacyclin opposes platelet thromboxane A2. Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase; anucleate platelets cannot replace it, but endothelial cells can, so low doses shift the balance toward prostacyclin. Endothelin-1, one of the most potent endogenous vasoconstrictors, is cleaved from big endothelin by endothelin converting enzyme and mainly secreted as it is made. Hypoxia, angiotensin II, and thrombin increase it; NO, prostacyclin, and laminar shear suppress it, and endothelial ETB receptors release NO and clear it. It is increased in pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Weibel-Palade bodies are rod shaped endothelial granules of von Willebrand factor (vWF) with P-selectin in their membrane, released within minutes by thrombin, histamine, epinephrine, or vasopressin acting on V2 receptors. vWF bridges exposed collagen to platelet glycoprotein Ib, essential at high shear, and carries factor VIII, so severe vWF deficiency lowers factor VIII. ADAMTS13 trims ultralarge vWF multimers; its deficiency lets them aggregate platelets in small vessels, causing thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Preformed P-selectin starts leukocyte rolling within minutes, whereas E-selectin is synthesized over hours after interleukin 1 or tumor necrosis factor.

blocks.text: Endothelial dysfunction

Endothelial dysfunction is a shift in this balance, with reduced bioavailable NO as its hallmark. Hypertension, diabetes, smoking, oxidized LDL, hyperhomocysteinemia, and aging raise oxidative stress; superoxide destroys NO, and loss of tetrahydrobiopterin uncouples eNOS so it makes superoxide. ET-1, adhesion molecules (VCAM-1, ICAM-1, selectins), tissue factor, and PAI-1 rise and thrombomodulin falls. The vessel dilates poorly or constricts paradoxically, the surface becomes prothrombotic (the endothelial injury of Virchow's triad), and monocytes and LDL enter the intima. Low, disturbed shear at branch points and curves explains where plaques form.

blocks.title: The self reinforcing cycle of endothelial dysfunction
steps: Risk factors raise endothelial oxidative stress
Superoxide destroys NO and eNOS uncouples
Adhesion molecules, ET-1, and LDL entry increase
Monocytes and oxidized LDL build an intimal lesion
The lesion generates more reactive oxygen species
blocks.caption: Each stage feeds the next, driving progression toward atherosclerosis.

integration.text: Embryology and anatomy explain placement. The endocardium is continuous with vascular endothelium because both line the primitive heart tube, and the AV rings form as connective tissue of the atrioventricular groove separates atrial from ventricular muscle; incomplete separation leaves an accessory pathway. Coronary arteries run in epicardial fat and penetrate inward, linking gross anatomy to subendocardial vulnerability. Wall structure maps onto hemodynamics (compliance, resistance, exchange, capacitance), and endothelial signals use familiar second messengers: cGMP for NO and natriuretic peptides, cAMP for prostacyclin, and IP3 with Ca2+ for endothelin-1.

Pathology reads as damage to a layer: atherosclerosis in the intima, cystic medial degeneration and Monckeberg calcification in the media, syphilitic aortitis through the adventitial vasa vasorum, and desmosomal or gap junction defects in the myocardium. Postcapillary venule selectins link the vessel wall to every acute inflammatory response. A key limit is that light microscopy shows structure, not function: a normal looking endothelium can be profoundly dysfunctional, which is detected by its response to flow or acetylcholine.

summary: The heart wall has an endocardium with a subendocardial layer carrying Purkinje fibers, a myocardium whose thickness follows chamber pressure, and an epicardium carrying the coronary vessels in fat.

Wall stress is proportional to pressure times radius divided by twice the wall thickness, so pressure overload causes concentric hypertrophy and dilation without thickening sharply raises myocyte stress.
The subendocardium is injured first in ischemia because its supply arrives last, its vessels are compressed in systole, and its wall stress is highest.
The collagenous fibrous skeleton anchors the valves and insulates atria from ventricles, so the bundle of His through the central fibrous body is the only normal electrical link.

Cardiac myocytes are branched, with central nuclei, abundant mitochondria, diads at the Z line, and intercalated discs whose fascia adherens and desmosomes couple force and whose connexin 43 gap junctions make a functional syncytium.
Adult cardiomyocytes are essentially postmitotic, so the heart adapts by hypertrophy and heals infarcts by scar.

Purkinje fibers are large, pale, glycogen rich subendocardial cells with sparse myofibrils built for the fastest conduction; atrial myocytes store ANP, which acts through cGMP to promote natriuresis and vasodilation.
Elastic arteries recoil in diastole, muscular arteries distribute flow, and arterioles set resistance through the inverse fourth power of radius.
Capillary permeability rises from continuous to fenestrated to sinusoidal; veins are compliant capacitance vessels, and postcapillary venules are the site of leukocyte emigration.

Endothelial NO and prostacyclin relax vessels and inhibit platelets, endothelin-1 constricts, and Weibel-Palade bodies release vWF and P-selectin; endothelial dysfunction tips the balance toward constriction, thrombosis, and atherosclerosis.

verify: Normal wall thickness values (left ventricle about 1.3 to 1.5 cm, right ventricle about 0.3 to 0.5 cm) follow Robbins; other texts give a left ventricular range of about 1.0 to 1.5 cm.

Cardiomyocyte dimensions, the fraction of cell volume occupied by mitochondria (stated as about a third or more), and the number of elastic lamellae in the aortic media (about 40 to 70) vary between histology texts.
The statement that ANP granules are most numerous in the right atrium follows standard histology texts; confirm whether NABNE tests the right versus left atrial distribution.
The idea that Purkinje fiber glycogen improves tolerance to ischemia is a widely taught explanation rather than a precisely quantified finding; it is phrased cautiously here.
The arteriole size cutoff varies between texts (about 0.1 mm in some, up to about 0.3 to 0.5 mm in others).
Conduction velocities (Purkinje fibers about 1.5 to 4 m/s, ventricular muscle about 0.3 to 0.5 m/s, AV node about 0.05 m/s) and the arteriolar pressure values are approximate consensus figures.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Monckeberg, Naxos disease, Weibel-Palade, and bundle of Kent, and the valve layer names fibrosa and spongiosa, or only descriptive terms.
